title: Colleen Chien, Miriam Kim & Breon Austin — the generative-AI-and-legal-aid field study, discussed with a participating clinic
pub: Talk Justice, An LSC Podcast, episode 84, host Cat Moon (Vanderbilt), YouTube / Legal Talk Network
author: Colleen Chien · Miriam Kim · Breon Austin

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The source accepts that AI has meaningful access-to-justice potential but that access or uptake alone is insufficient. It materially develops the proposition with pilot-based observations on uneven uptake, risk-sensitive task selection, verification, affordability, informed consent and collaborative learning, while not establishing sustained or system-wide justice-gap reduction.
qs: So again, I think this idea that there is a lot of promise, but we have to be thoughtful about how we deploy it, is something that came across that said when people did use the technology, they really appreciated it.
But if it’s used in a way where precision is not that important, then it can be deployed in a way that actually saves people time rather than creates more work.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core account of selective, human-led deployment and materially extends it with field evidence from legal-aid clinics: training and responsive support improved use, while task selection was explicitly calibrated to verification burden and precision. It also develops the access-to-justice dimension through informed-consent, affordability and direct-to-consumer quality safeguards.
qs: People found it useful, they could do it, they could use it for a lot of different reasons, and that assistance actually improved the outcomes.

So I think that’s why we tried to start again with our pilot with legal aid lawyers who do have the training to verify the accuracy, but also to explore use cases where legal citations aren’t necessary.

st.t: Court AI: Existing failures set the comparison
st.an: The source supports assessing consumer-facing court and legal-aid AI against the inadequacy of existing one-to-one provision and unmet legal need, rather than against ideal human service. It also reinforces the synthesis’s caution that potential scale does not establish effectiveness and that deployment depends on verification, affordability, regulatory reform and informed consent.
qs: Well, I think one of the greatest opportunities is figuring out how we can scale this technology, to your point, Colleen, to be consumer facing, to really scale what right now is still a very one-to-one service model and is woefully inadequate and will remain.
And again, I’m always going to talk about informed consent and making sure everyone understands what’s going on and agrees to it.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s calibrated position: direct-to-consumer legal technology is already being used and therefore requires certification or quality controls, while lawyer productivity gains alone cannot close the justice gap. It favors legal-aid-lawyer-directed technology rather than treating unsupervised AI or efficiency improvements as sufficient.
qs: And so if we know that that’s the case, we need to think about how to certify or have some sort of quality standard that’s available for these offerings.
And I will say from an access to justice perspective, even if we were able to double the productivity of every legal aid lawyer, we’d still have a huge gap.

st.t: Justice augmentation: Activity exceeds proven access gains
st.an: The source supports AI as a potential means of expanding access to justice while stressing that equalising gains require deliberate investigation, training and shared learning rather than being assumed. Its field study and use-case resource demonstrate organised activity, but the supplied evidence does not establish measured access or legal-outcome improvements, matching the cluster’s caution that activity exceeds proven gains.
qs: And I really want to encourage the broader legal community to be thinking that way and to be putting on trainings to enable the next generation to also learn as they’re coming into the legal practice and just all work together to share our learnings to increase access to justice.

st.t: Justice capacity: AI potential requires deliberate implementation
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central proposition that AI’s access-to-justice potential requires deliberate engagement rather than technology alone. It also reinforces the implementation agenda through training and shared learning, while offering resources and use cases rather than evidence of improved access outcomes.
qs: And I really want to encourage the broader legal community to be thinking that way and to be putting on trainings to enable the next generation to also learn as they’re coming into the legal practice and just all work together to share our learnings to increase access to justice.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source directly supports selective, risk-sensitive augmentation: legal-aid practitioners found AI useful when deployment was thoughtful and concentrated on uses where lower precision requirements made verification manageable. It also reinforces the cluster’s claims that benefits depend on implementation and that access alone does not ensure equitable uptake.
qs: So again, I think this idea that there is a lot of promise, but we have to be thoughtful about how we deploy it, is something that came across that said when people did use the technology, they really appreciated it.
But if it’s used in a way where precision is not that important, then it can be deployed in a way that actually saves people time rather than creates more work.

kp.k: AI equalization requires deliberate deployment rather than market diffusion
kp.d: Colleen Chien argues that AI's equalizing promise will not deliver itself: regulatory concern and commercial development have not put equality at the forefront. Miriam Kim traces the project to the California State Bar approaching Berkeley in spring 2023 after funding and political battles limited its technology-and-access-to-justice work.
qs: if we want to deliver on the promise of AI being an equalizer, we need to actually deliberately engage in that question.
they approached Berkeley Law School in the spring of 2023 because they had lost the ability to really pursue that as they had been in the past due to some funding and political battles

kp.k: Randomized support intervention reportedly improved participants' experience
kp.d: Kim describes a randomized control trial comparing support while using AI tools against no support and reports a meaningful difference in experience; Chien says assistance improved outcomes. The transcript supplies no sample size, effect size, detailed outcome measures or follow-up period, so these are interview reports of findings rather than a full presentation of trial evidence.
qs: we wanted to see if there was a difference if you gave people support while they were using the tools versus not, would you see some meaningful difference in their experience? And we found that it did.
that assistance actually improved the outcomes.

kp.k: Initial gender disparity disappeared after providing tool access
kp.d: Chien reports that about 75% of legal aid professionals and lawyers are women, yet most use in the surveyed legal aid population was by men. She says no gender difference remained once the project deployed tools and provided access. She interprets this as evidence of uneven organic uptake, familiarity or trust, not equalization through availability alone; numerical subgroup results are not provided.
qs: about 75% of legal aid professionals and lawyers are women.
when we took the survey among those folks who were in the legal aid profession, most of the use was by men.
once we actually deployed the technology and gave folks access to the tools, there was really no difference in gender.

kp.k: Practitioner-directed deployment responds to unauthorized-practice restrictions
kp.d: Kim says California unauthorized-practice-of-law regulations constrained developers' consumer-facing legal tools, motivating initial deployment through legal aid lawyers and clinic supervisors. She recommends funding, training and support for frontline professionals, with their experience feeding back to developers. This is supervised augmentation rather than direct reliance by consumers.
qs: in California we still have unauthorized practice of law regulations that limit developers’ ability to create consumer facing legal technology tools.
we can then create a feedback loop back to the developers.
this is going to require funding to get the tools and the hands of those on the front lines, but also requires training and support.

kp.k: Risk-sensitive task selection can preserve net time savings
kp.d: Chien argues that pilot participants reconciled law's precision requirements with AI's limitations by choosing uses where risks were manageable and precision less critical. Kim identifies ordinary dispute-resolution letters to landlords, agencies or other parties as examples that need not contain legal citations. These are proposed lower-risk applications, not findings that AI legal research is reliably accurate.
qs: they used it in ways where they can manage the risk.
if it’s used in a way where precision is not that important, then it can be deployed in a way that actually saves people time rather than creates more work.
sometimes people came in needing a letter. It wasn’t a legal brief, it was really a letter that even a non-lawyer could write.

kp.k: Clinic time savings supported deeper human client interaction
kp.d: Participating pro bono manager Bréyon Austin describes approximately hour-long clinic appointments, much of which clients' narratives consume. She contrasts 20 minutes or more researching local rules and ordinances before AI with almost instantaneous tool results, followed by human checking. Her practitioner account links faster research and drafting to more time for client connection and clients feeling heard; it is not presented as a quantified trial outcome.
qs: we have about an hour to meet with a client.
an attorney could spend 20 minutes or more before the use of these tools researching local rules and ordinances
using these AI tools, your results were almost instantaneous.
having the use of these tools to speed up and make things more efficient gave us way more time to just have a deep connection with the clients.

kp.k: Hallucination makes human verification central to safe use
kp.d: Kim identifies hallucination as her largest concern because fast, confident outputs can discourage doubt. Busy lawyers may lack time to verify, while self-represented litigants may not know how. She explains that starting with trained legal aid lawyers was a safeguard; Austin likewise insists on checking results. No measured hallucination rate is given.
qs: the biggest concern is hallucination
the output tends to come very quickly and come in a manner that exudes confidence, that gives you no reason to doubt its accuracy.
that poses risks if you’re a busy lawyer who doesn’t have time to verify, or if you’re a pro state litigant who doesn’t know how to verify.
please due diligence, check your results, check the work

kp.k: Embedded support suggests a technology-focused pro bono model
kp.d: Austin credits Kim's training and participation in the clinic with making tool use possible. Chien proposes that lawyers trained on AI in their firms transfer knowledge and access to pro bono partners. She describes a concierge model involving Kim and students providing on-call help, office hours and email responses, distinguishing timely, tailored assistance from simply offering databases or additional training calls.
qs: having Miriam participate in the clinic with us and show us how to use a lot of these tools was just really huge.
if lawyers are being trained in their law firms and getting access to all these kind of great tools, they can work with the pro bono organizations that they’re working with
Miriam and a team of students, they were on call, they did office hours, they did, they responded to emails.

kp.k: Shared use cases and peer communities support adoption
kp.d: Host Cat Moon describes a database of a hundred use cases rated for efficiency, usefulness and likely reuse. Chien emphasizes peer demonstration, reported time savings and positive initial experiences. Kim describes One Justice's existing convening activity and proposes recurring exchanges and founder-supported free pilots lasting perhaps six months or a year; those longer pilots and a dedicated recurring AI community are aspirations, not established study results.
qs: you share a database of a hundred use cases all rated in terms of the efficiency gain and how useful it was, whether it’s likely to be replicated.
when we asked folks, tell us your best use cases that they also told us how much time did they save and would they reuse it
my dream would be that there would also be legal tech founders who are willing to support this effort
maybe for six months or a year to really try to explore the potential here.

kp.k: Continued clinic adoption depends on consent and affordability
kp.d: Austin reports continued weekly clinic use after the pilot and exploration of applications outside the clinic, with clients consulted before tool use. She identifies fear of new technology and potentially unaffordable tools for legal service organizations and self-represented parties as adoption barriers, and recommends further law-firm/legal-services pilot partnerships.
qs: We have our clinic weekly and we’re still using the AI tools.
we check in with each client before using the tools.
Some of these tools just may be too expensive for legal service organizations and for self-represented parties.
law firms have an incredible opportunity to partner with legal service organizations to further explore the use of these AI tools.

kp.k: Consumer tools require quality standards alongside regulatory change
kp.d: Chien argues that consumers already use AI directly, making certification or quality standards necessary, especially for legal aid bots. She acknowledges tensions around legitimizing consumer offerings under unauthorized-practice rules. She also argues that even doubling legal aid lawyer productivity would leave substantial unmet need because people may not know about, access or conveniently use available help.
qs: a lot of consumers are going to be using these technologies directly, not only just through and under the supervision of attorneys.
we need to think about how to certify or have some sort of quality standard that’s available for these offerings.
even if we were able to double the productivity of every legal aid lawyer, we’d still have a huge gap.

kp.k: Expungement example suggests scale beyond conventional legal aid
kp.d: Chien cites her expungement work, stating that one in three adults has a criminal record and many could clear it but lack easy access to tools. As an illustration of lawyer-directed technology and regulatory flexibility, she relays Rasa's founder's account of serving thousands—tentatively recalling 10,000—in its first Utah year, versus hundreds served by all legal aid the preceding year. This is a secondhand scale comparison, not a field-study finding or a demonstrated causal effect of generative AI.
qs: one in three adults has a criminal record, many of them could get it cleared

in the first year of their operations in Utah, which has kind of a looser regulatory environment with a sandbox, she was able to serve thousands, I think 10,000 people, whereas the entirety of legal aid in the previous year was in the hundreds.
we need to solve this unauthorized practice of law issues so that we can make and enable these technologies to be out there

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The speakers describe supported, lawyer-supervised AI use as a way to improve legal-aid efficiency and client contact, while arguing that equalizing access requires deliberate deployment and approaches beyond lawyer productivity alone.
pts.d: Miriam Kim reports that providing support alongside AI tools made a meaningful difference to participants’ experience. Colleen Chien reports uneven initial uptake by gender, despite women constituting about 75% of legal-aid professionals and lawyers, but no gender difference once participants received access to the tools. Bréyon Austin describes faster research and drafting in a clinic, freeing time for human connection with clients. Chien argues that selecting tasks with lower precision requirements can deliver time savings rather than additional checking work. Kim identifies ordinary dispute-resolution letters as one such use. Chien proposes a pro bono model in which law-firm lawyers transfer tool access and skills to legal-aid organizations, and argues that peer demonstrations encourage adoption. She also predicts substantial direct consumer use and argues that even doubling legal-aid lawyers’ productivity would leave a large justice gap; she therefore calls for quality standards and attention to regulatory barriers affecting consumer-facing services. These are claims about augmentation and broader access, not findings that AI can replace lawyers or close the justice gap by itself.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists of a reported randomized pilot, an uptake survey, participant-reported use cases, and clinic experience; the podcast does not provide detailed statistical results.
pts.d: Chien describes the pilot as a randomized control trial, and Kim explains that it compared experiences with and without support. The episode reports a positive support effect but gives no sample size, effect size, confidence interval, or detailed outcome definitions. Chien’s gender-uptake claim draws on a survey followed by experience during deployment. The accompanying collection of 100 use cases records reported time savings and willingness to reuse applications rather than an independently measured legal-accuracy benchmark. Austin supplies firsthand clinic testimony: tasks that could previously take 20 minutes or more produced almost instantaneous initial results, with verification still necessary. She also reports that hands-on training and assistance were crucial. Chien offers Rasa as a scaling example, relaying its founder’s account of serving thousands—tentatively about 10,000—in its first Utah year, compared with hundreds served by legal aid in the preceding year. This is a secondhand account offered by Chien, not a measured result of the generative-AI pilot or an established generative-AI effect. The proposed pro bono model, certification, and broader scaling arguments are recommendations or expectations rather than demonstrated outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The reported benefits concern an early pilot and continuing clinic use by the 2024 discussion; wider gains are conditional on support, affordability, verification, consent, suitable tasks, and regulatory arrangements.
pts.d: Kim dates the initiating approach to Berkeley to spring 2023; the transcript does not specify the pilot’s exact dates or duration. Austin says the clinic continued using AI weekly at the time of the discussion and was exploring applications outside the clinic. The speakers do not set a deadline for closing the justice gap. Kim says frontline deployment requires funding, training, and support, and explains that California unauthorized-practice restrictions shaped the decision to place tools with legal-aid lawyers rather than directly with consumers. Hallucination remains a central qualification: confident output can be inaccurate, lawyers may lack time to verify it, and self-represented people may lack the skills. Austin emphasizes checking results and obtaining informed consent. Chien’s time-saving argument is specifically conditional on risk-manageable uses, especially those not requiring high precision. Austin identifies expense and fear of new technology as adoption barriers. Kim’s suggestion of free six-month or one-year vendor pilots is a prospective implementation proposal, not the duration of the reported trial.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are legal-aid staff and volunteers, underserved and self-represented clients, law-firm pro bono teams, developers, and consumers using legal tools directly.
pts.d: Kim and Chien place legal-aid lawyers and other frontline professionals at the center of supported adoption: tools may make their work more productive, while responsive assistance reduces learning burdens. Austin’s example concerns the Lawyers Committee for Civil Rights of the San Francisco Bay Area’s free drop-in clinic, where volunteers have about an hour per client. She reports that faster work enables clients to receive help while feeling heard, respected, and connected; this is participant testimony, not a separately measured client-outcome result. Women in legal aid are relevant to Chien’s finding that organic uptake was uneven, whereas supported access showed no gender difference. Law-firm lawyers are positioned as potential training and tool-access partners, rather than as workers shown to be displaced. Developers could receive feedback from frontline use and support longer free trials. Direct consumers and self-represented litigants face affordability and verification risks, motivating Chien’s call for quality standards. People unable to access conventional legal aid, including those seeking record clearance, are the intended beneficiaries of scalable offerings beyond the one-to-one lawyer model.
